work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In illud: Quando ipsi subiciet omnia

paragraphs.text: Yesterday, brothers, we spoke about the endless kingdom of Christ. Our sermon came at the height of your attention, and it gave the listeners a sufficient proof. By "sufficient" I mean sufficient for the strength of the preacher, not for the worth of what is preached. For there is nothing on earth or in heaven that can worthily praise the much-praised dignity of the Only-begotten. The prophets proclaimed many things in advance about the Lord's divine appearing, the law ordained many things, the apostles preached many things, the evangelists recounted many things, and none of them has been able to reach his worth. If so many rivers of the Holy Spirit, whose streams are ever-flowing and pure, emptied out all human power and still uttered nothing worthy of the divine power, where will the tiniest drop of speech show itself, when a subject of such worth is set before it? A mortal tongue cannot worthily praise an immortal nature, and human speech has no room to praise worthily the Word of God who made the world. What then? We preach as far as we are able, since we cannot do as much as we ought. In other contests the winners carry off the crowns, but in the labours of theology it is those who confess themselves defeated who carry off the crowns of right-mindedness. So let us be defeated by speaking, rather than condemned for keeping silent.

Now the endlessness of the kingdom has been shown, as [?] someone says, and so has the statement that he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, that is, the world that was once ruled by sin and later came to be ruled by grace. But the words "When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him" were left unexamined. So it is necessary to say what we can, so that our silence does not become a stumbling-block for the ill-disposed. All of you should know, brothers, that we did not leave this out on purpose. We thought we had delivered a complete and well-examined account, and that what remained had been made clear by what came before. For one purpose and one principle both resolves the earlier passage and clarifies the present one: the apostle said these things by way of accommodation. There, the words about handing over the kingdom to God the Father did not agree with the force of the proclamation; the expression was introduced on the surface because of the weakness of those who had been rescued from the error of many gods ("I gave you milk to drink, not solid food"). In the same way, and on the same principle, this too is said now. Everywhere the apostle's purpose is to show that the divine nature is never at odds with itself, and that the Son does not stand against the Father, as the Jews impiously supposed. For they said, "This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath." So he presents one nature free from strife, one concord, one word, one will, one authority, one God in all, so as to cut off the shoots of the error of many gods. For we have shown, as the diligent among the listeners remember, that the same passage which bears witness to the dignity of the Father proclaims the dignity of Christ in the very same words and syllables. Just as it said there, "so that God may be all in all," so too of the Only-begotten: "but Christ is all in all." What, then, does "will be subjected" mean? He is preparing a remedy for the pagan disease. He is not introducing a doctrine of the Church; he is driving out a pagan notion. And if we must give a plain explanation, he means the subjection of Christ that comes about through the Church. For when the Church is subjected, having nothing spurious or counterfeit in it, but offering God a sincere and genuine disposition, then he will truly be subjected to him.

"That explanation is forced," someone says, "and not enough to persuade the ill-disposed." Well then, so that you may learn that everything of this sort which is ascribed to Christ is to be seen in Christ's Church, I will bring before you the Master of the Church himself as witness. But let me begin a little further back, so that what I say may be clear. While Christ was in this world in the flesh, fulfilling the human dispensation for the salvation of the world, the Saviour of the world was persecuted by the Jews and hounded by the enemies of the truth, and the source of all kindness was treated with ingratitude by those who enjoyed his kindness. But when he had fulfilled the whole dispensation through his passion, he passed to the heavenly choirs. In his body he departed, but in his dignity he fills all things. He took up on high the body he had put on and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. He did not receive some strange and foreign glory; he clothed the mortal body with that great dignity. After the ascension, then, and his release from sufferings, after that much-praised resurrection and his passing into heaven, he was worshipped by the whole host above the heavens, with the entire angelic guard standing around him. He was no longer among the afflicted, or the persecuted, or the hounded. Yet when he saw Paul raging against the Church and pouring out great fury against the saints, the one who after his passion was persecuted nowhere, but lived in such honour and divine glory, said to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And yet I am not persecuting you, for you hold the place of honour in heaven. "Why are you persecuting me?" He makes the sufferings of the Church his own. "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" Do you see that the persecution of the Church is credited to Christ, the head of the Church? Just as he says that he himself is persecuted when the Church is persecuted, so now Paul says that Christ is subjected when the Church is subjected.

Take another proof of the argument as well: "for every word shall be established by two or three witnesses." It is not that the Master's voice needs further testimony. But when Christ speaks, he is believed by believers and is unconvincing to unbelievers. We are not strengthening the Master's voice; we are stopping the mouth of heretical ill-will. This Paul learned from Christ himself that the persecution of the Church refers to Christ. Knowing, then, that whatever the Church suffers is referred to Christ, he followed in the footsteps of the King's words and says somewhere in one of his letters, "I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ." Is Christ, then, still afflicted after going up to heaven? But look at what follows: "I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ in my flesh, for the sake of his body, which is the Church." Do you see how Christ makes the Church's sufferings and honour his own? Have you honoured the Church? You have honoured Christ. Have you persecuted the Church? Even if not to his face, yet by your intention you have persecuted Christ. Consider how great is the danger for those who grieve the Church, and how great the crown for those who honour the Church. "Whoever rejects you rejects me," says the Saviour. I recognize that voice, O Master: it follows the pattern of the Father. For the Father too spoke this way about his prophets of old, making the insult done to the righteous his own. When Abimelech, the king of the Philistines, took Sarah, Abraham's wife, God said to him, "Return the man's wife, for he is a prophet and will pray for you." Abimelech defended himself and said, "Lord, I did not know that she was his wife; I did this with a pure heart." And what did God say to him? "I too knew that you did this with a pure heart; that is why I spared you from sinning against me." It has been shown, then, brothers, that everything seen in the Church refers to Christ. So the apostle says, "The Son" (that is, the Church) "will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him."

But the ill-disposed man has another way out. "What?" he says. "Is the Church not subjected now, but will be subjected only then, after the resurrection?" The same refutation applies to your objection, heretic. Tell me: by your own argument, is Christ not subjected now? The words "When all things are subjected to him, then he will be subjected" would have had a point if he were not already subjected at present. But if, by your argument, heretic, he is always in subjection and never resists the Father, then "When all things are subjected to him, then he will be subjected" is superfluous. You cite his subjection against him in countless phrases, and then you store up yet a second subjection of his for another time? If you hear Christ saying, "I did not come to do my own will, but the will of the one who sent me," you immediately thrust out the horn of impiety and say, "Do you see how he is subjected to the Father?" If you hear him saying, "I do not speak on my own; the Father has given me a command, what to say and what to speak," you immediately seize on the phrase and insist that Christ has no authority of his own but is subjected. If you hear him saying, "I judge no one; there is one who seeks and judges," you immediately snatch his subjection from the phrase. Since by all these passages you show him to be subjected, why do you bring in an ill-disposed argument and say, "I follow the wording and not the sense," claiming that the one who is always subjected will be subjected then? What, then, is the sense? Everywhere the apostle's purpose is to abolish the error of many gods, to remove the strife attributed to the nature that knows no strife, and to banish the suspicions of those who think wrongly. So he shows a subjection that is not forced, not compelled, not servile, but one that fits the concord of their equal dignity.

But, brother, do not let anything in what was said before trip you up, such as "I do not say this on my own; the Father has given me a command, what to say and what to speak." I am afraid that you may take what is said in combat against the heretics as Church doctrine, and set aside the sense of the proclamation. In the previous sermon our argument insisted, in defence of the apostolic meaning, that the apostles do not preach everything as doctrine, but put forward some things as doctrine and others by way of accommodation. In the same way I find that the very source of truth, the Master of the apostles and prophets, does not always speak as doctrine in keeping with his own dignity, but by way of accommodation stoops down to the weakness of the people. Tell me, brother: when the Master of truth says, "If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true," shall I follow the wording? Shall I follow the bare phrase? Shall I insult his dignity because of his accommodation? But even if I wanted to be ill-disposed, the Master would not allow me. He will shut out my wrong thinking if I follow the wording wrongly, and he takes me up on my words as speaking falsely about holy things, as confusing and insulting his dignity without a second thought. For he says: "Because I stooped down to the Jews and said, 'If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true,' have you snatched the phrase for blasphemy? Did you not hear me say elsewhere, 'Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true'?" What then, brothers? Does truth contradict itself? Certainly not! It speaks one way to those raised with the truth and another way to those cut off from the truth. It does not change itself; it adapts itself to people's dispositions. Why, then, does he say to the Jews, "I do not speak on my own; the Father has given me a command, what to say and what to speak"? Because they thought he was an enemy of the law of Moses, giving commands contrary to the Father, who honoured the sabbath through the law, and on the surface the new covenant seemed to be opposing the old order. So, wishing to show that he was not opposing God and was not preaching against the law, he says, "I do not speak on my own" (as you suppose), "but he himself has given me a command," the one you worship. He all but teaches them: "If you set these things aside, it is not my teaching you are setting aside; you are offending the God you yourselves confess." Otherwise, brothers, suppose I took Christ's word so pitifully, so meanly, so basely as to understand in a servile sense the voice that says, "I do nothing on my own; the Father has given me commands, what to say and what to speak." Do you see how deep into impiety I would sink by understanding it this way? I would make him not only inferior to the Father but even lesser than the apostles. Hear how. Paul says, "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion." Does Paul speak without a command, while Christ cannot say anything on his own? "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion." Do you allow Paul to give his opinion even without a command, yet shut Christ up under the yoke of slavery, following the wording that says, "I speak nothing on my own"? Then again, as I said a moment ago, he speaks one way to those raised with the truth and another way to those cut off from it. Did the Jews suppose him to be the Son of God? Did the Jews have any notion of God the Word? Have you not heard what they say about him? "This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath." They did not think him even a man of God; did they conceive of the dignity of the Only-begotten? Again, the same people said of the Saviour, "We know that this man is a sinner, because he does not keep the sabbath." Holding the opinion that he was a sinner, a man cut off from the truth, could they have had room for even the faintest notion of divinity at all?

To people of that disposition he lowered his voice. He taught them not to oppose the form they saw, which they supposed was at variance with God's will, and said, "I do not speak on my own; he himself has given me a command, what to say and what to speak." But see how, with the children of faith, he lays aside that lowly speech, puts on the authority of divine dignity, and says, "You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not commit adultery.' Whoever looks at his neighbour's wife with desire has already sinned. But I say..." Do you see how, where the listener is faithful, there is naked authority, but where the listener is suspicious, the teaching is shaped for accommodation?

When a small child was crushed in the crowd, he said: "Disturbance always springs up while the divine word is being heard. For the devil, the enemy of souls, sees the word sending sharpened arrows against his error, and so he keeps stirring up the listeners, in order to escape the refutation of the truth. A young man named Eutychus disturbed Paul's teaching, and here too a youngster has disturbed the people's listening, so that the listeners' resolve may be tested all the more. But you, brothers, escape the tossing of the waves, and let us bring our boat to anchor in the calm harbour of the truth. For I do not want this digression to run on and hinder what lies before us."

Where the listener is suspicious, the teaching is shaped for accommodation; where there is a true companion of piety, there is naked authority. To the Jews he says, "I speak nothing on my own." To those who belong to the faith he says, "You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I say..." The "I" shows the authority of the speaker. Everywhere the "I" bears witness to the speaker's authority, as when he says, "I am, I am, and until you grow old, I am." And again he says to the Jews, "I did not come to do my own will, but the will of the one who sent me." Today's reading from the Gospels resolves the difficulty raised by the heretics' notion. When the leper came to him (leprous in body but radiant in soul), he said to him, "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean." Look for the heretics' rule here. He ought then, in keeping with his own saying, to have said, "I do not will it; the Father wills it. Be clean. For I did not come to do my own will, but the will of the one who sent me. Have you not heard me say, 'I did not come to do my own will'?" If, then, as the impious argue, you force his will to be subject to another's authority, why do you ask for authority from one who is subject to the Father's authority? But the Saviour said none of this to the man who came to him sincerely. He accepted the sincerity of his faith and gave him a sincere and genuine healing: "You came to me in faith; receive the remedy in faith. You credit the kindness to my will; receive your healing from my will." "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean." "I will it; be clean." Does the heretics' impious rule still stand? Do you see that he is subject in word, but acts with authority by his own will?

When I say this, I am not presenting the will of the Son as cut off from the will of the Father. Whatever you call the will of the Son, you are calling the will of the Father; whatever you call the will of the Father, you are proclaiming the authority of the Son; and if you speak of the authority of the Son, you are declaring the authority of the Holy Spirit. For the authority is one, and the kingdom undivided. "But you have passed over the authority of the Spirit," someone says. "For I find from the apostle's words that the Spirit is subjected to Christ. Paul said, 'But when it says that all things are subjected to him, it is clear that this excludes the one who subjected all things to him.' If it excludes only the one who subjected them, then is not the Spirit subjected? For he said that only the Father is not subjected to Christ." The words "all things" refer to creation; they do not insult the uncreated nature. He is speaking about the subjection of enemies: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death." Why, then, do you put the Holy Spirit in the place of the subjected enemies? Did the Father bring in a subjection of friends? Did he mention a subjection of angels? Did he touch on a subjection of archangels? It is a subjection of enemies. "The last enemy to be destroyed is death." The Holy Spirit is not among the subjected enemies. If we believers, who believe in Christ, will reign with him, will the Holy Spirit not attain even the same dignity as his subjects? At the Saviour's appearing the sons of Zebedee, James and John, and the company of the apostles will sit on twelve thrones, and will the Spirit be down by the footstool among the subjected? Turn away from impiety! The passage is about creation, sir, not about the uncreated nature, not about the dignity that is worshipped.

And so that you may receive an exact and well-examined account of true religion, consider how blessed David, when he brings in the choir of creation singing praise, says, "Praise the Lord from the heavens, praise him in the heights," and what follows: angels, powers, heavens of heavens, and the water above the heavens. Did he mention the Spirit? Did he count the uncreated nature along with creation? The three young men with Ananias in the furnace likewise brought in the choir of creation, saying, "Sing praise, angels of the Lord, heavens of the Lord, powers of the Lord, sun and moon," and what follows. Did they mention the Holy Spirit? Did they count the Uncreated along with creation? Again, Paul, distinguishing the invisible things from the visible, teaches somewhere, "For in Christ all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible," and he at once lists the invisible things, saying, "whether thrones or dominions or principalities or authorities." All visible things are admitted to be servants, but among the invisible there are angels and powers, and also the Holy Spirit and the Son and the Father. So that you would not, through ignorance of the order of heaven, drag the lordly dignity of the divine Spirit under the yoke of slavery, he does not break down the visible things or say, "whether sun or moon or stars, all are servants." Their status is admitted: "all things are your servants." But among the invisible things were principalities and angels, and the Spirit who is worshipped was also invisible. So that no one would include him among the invisible things, he lists all the things above, to remove the Lord from the rank of servants. He lists those that worship, to set apart the one who is worshipped: "whether thrones or principalities or authorities." He did not say, "or the Spirit."

But let us come to the matter before us. "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean." The leper saw kindness gushing forth; he saw healing welling up; he saw many who were sick and possessed by demons crowding around the source of healing. So he laid aside any division in his mind, leprous in body but clean in soul. For his soul was not divided into different colours. Just as leprosy is repulsive in the body because it splits up the skin's colour, so a double heart is repulsive in the soul, divided between faith and unbelief. As much as leprosy repels human eyes by its appearance, so much does a divided soul repel the eyes of God. That is why Scripture says, "Woe to a double heart and a slack soul, and to the sinner who walks on two paths." But let us return to the matter before us. "I will it; be clean." What a wonder! "I will it; be clean." There is, brothers, a word that is often spoken with authority, and often also out of boastfulness. Anyone at all can utter it, but only one who has the power can make the deed follow the authority. If he had said "I will it" and no deed had followed, it would have been boasting. But as it is, the deed followed the word. So do not cavil at the word; stand in awe of the deed.

See how great the difference is between the old law and the new grace in every respect. When Moses came down from the mountain, with his first legislation and first law he ordered that lepers be put outside the camp; when Christ came down from the mountain, he at once cleansed a leper. The one banishes the afflictions, the other heals them. Christ went up a mountain, and Moses went up too: the one to receive the law, the other to give it. Moses went up and found the mountain full of trumpets, cloud, thunder, lightning, storm and darkness. This was not because these things befitted the glory [?] of the One who appeared, but because they were training the people in reverence. But the grace of Christ, brothers, lays aside fear and casts out slavery. For we did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear; we received a spirit of adoption. Moses gave ten commandments, but Jesus, the Master of Moses, gave nine beatitudes. All who are familiar with the Scriptures know that this is true. The first beatitude: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted. Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God. Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when they revile you and persecute you and falsely say every kind of evil against you.”

Why, then, does the law have ten commandments, while grace has nine beatitudes? The number of the ten commandments matches the number of plagues sent against the Egyptians: ten plagues against the Egyptians to chasten their arrogance, ten commandments for the people to correct their dullness. And the very letter by which the number ten is written, brothers, the iota I mean, has the shape and form of a rod. For it was a rod that chastised both the Egyptians and the people. But Jesus our Lord gives nine beatitudes, weaving the crown of beatitudes into a threefold strand from a triple triad. For, brothers, the worshipful Trinity, the royal dignity, the undefiled nature, the lordship that has no lord over it, has its glory in the Trinity; and so on earth God honors both the proclamation and the number of the virtues when it equals the number of the Holy Trinity. Here is what I mean. There were many patriarchs, yet God calls himself the God of the patriarchs: “I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.” This is not because he was not the God of Moses, or not the God of Joseph. For he is the God of all who call on him in truth. But he honors heavenly things in earthly ones, as in an image. Three patriarchs, in honor of the Trinity; three virtues, in honor of the Trinity: “And now these three remain: faith, hope, love.” Creation is divided into three, into the ranks of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth. Time is cut into three: past, present and future. And just as there were many patriarchs, yet three sufficed for the glorification of the Spirit, so, though there were many priests, a triad of priests is chosen: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel.” Many kings, many priests, and three are the ones remembered: “For except for David and Hezekiah and Josiah,” says Scripture, “all sinned.” In the furnace, three young men; with Christ on the mountain, Peter, James and John. There are many angels in heaven, and three appear to Abraham. All days are God’s, and three serve the mystery of Christ. Which three? “Take Isaac, your only son, whom you love, and go to one of the mountains.” And Abraham journeyed three days and three nights, so as to reveal the mystery at the same time; for he received Isaac back alive as if from the dead. Hear how. From the moment Isaac was taken to be sacrificed, he was dead to his father; for it is not the outcome of the deed but the intention that ratifies the promise. Isaac had been put to death by his father, as far as the intention went; on the third day he was given back alive, as a type of the resurrection. Jonah too could have spent many days in the sea, but he spends only three, to show the mystery of the resurrection.

Then someone says: “Even if you find testimonies like these scattered here and there, do you again take them as adequate [?] images of the Trinity and of the divine economy?” Do you reject these signs? If I am the one saying it, dismiss the argument; but if the proclamation is divine, hear it from me. Better, hear it along with me: the three days explain the Lord’s Passion. For concerning Abraham the Savior himself says: “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.” Which day? The day of his death. For the lamb that was given to Abraham from the tree bore the image of the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. To say “He saw the day” means nothing other than “He saw the death.” Where does this come from? We too often say of people, “His day has come,” meaning “His end.” But the law of common usage is not enough to confirm what is said. What then? Let us turn to Scripture. Blessed David says somewhere: “The sinner will watch the righteous and gnash his teeth at him, but the Lord will laugh at him, for he sees that his day is coming.” So much for Abraham. I will return to Jonah. Again, the three days of Jonah explain the saving Passion. Again the Savior himself proclaims this: “Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man must spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.” But in addition to what has been said, let us mention one thing stronger than the rest. The former people had three orders: priesthood, kingship and prophecy. Apart from these three offices, no other office could be seen among the Jews: kingship, priesthood, prophecy. There was a horn of oil, of sanctification. The anointing was one, but the gifts were three; one horn, three graces; for they anointed priests, kings and prophets. But since some do not know the subject, and so that my words may not run on in vain, wearing themselves out without benefiting the listener, hear it briefly. There was a horn kept by the prophets. From this horn kings, prophets and priests were anointed. The anointing did not change; rather, since the grace was supplied through the same horn, kings were anointed, priests were anointed, prophets were anointed: one anointing, three gifts. Why was the anointing oil in a horn? Because it bore the image of Christ. Could it not have been in a silver vessel? Could it not have been in gold? Could so great a gift not have been in some other, more precious material? But it was not; it was in a horn, because, as I said before, it bore the image of Christ. For “I will make a horn sprout for David.” May the Lord of priesthood, kingship and prophecy be with you all.
For once the chapter about the three men who were crushed into the horn had begun, he stopped.
